source.text: וַיְהִ֗י בִּימֵי֙ שְׁפֹ֣ט הַשֹּׁפְטִ֔ים וַיְהִ֥י רָעָ֖ב בָּאָ֑רֶץ וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ אִ֜ישׁ מִבֵּ֧ית לֶ֣חֶם יְהוּדָ֗ה לָגוּר֙ בִּשְׂדֵ֣י מוֹאָ֔ב ה֥וּא וְאִשְׁתּ֖וֹ וּשְׁנֵ֥י בָנָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was in [the] days of [the] judging of the judges, and there was a famine in the land; and went a man from Bethlehem [of] Judah to sojourn in [the] fields of Moab, he and his wife and [the] two of his sons.

en.L: And it came about in the days when the judges judged that there was a famine in the land. And a man from Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the fields of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons.
en.B: In the days when the judges judged, a famine struck the land. So a man from Bethlehem in Judah set out with his wife and his two sons to live for a while as an outsider in the country of Moab.
en.R: Long ago, in the time when judges led Israel, there was not enough food in the land. A man from the town of Bethlehem in Judah left to live for a time in the country of Moab. He took his wife and his two sons with him.

decisions.choice: in the days when the judges judged: the time between Joshua and the first kings
decisions.reason: The story is set in the age the book of Judges describes, after Israel entered the land and before it had a king (Judges 2:16-19; 21:25). The judges were leaders the LORD raised up to rescue Israel and govern it (see Judges 2:16). It was a time of unrest and of turning away from the LORD; against it this book tells of quiet loyalty in one family, which ends with the birth of David's grandfather (4:17-22).

decisions.choice: a famine in Bethlehem: hunger in the town whose name means house of bread
decisions.reason: The name Bethlehem means "house of bread" (or food). The story begins with no bread there, and turns when the LORD gives his people bread again (verse 6). The name is not explained in the text, but the contrast runs through the chapter: a full family leaves, and an empty widow comes back at harvest time (verses 21-22).

decisions.choice: to sojourn: to live as a resident outsider
decisions.reason: The verb is used of living for a time in a land not one's own, without the rights of a native, as Abraham did in Egypt during a famine (Genesis 12:10) and Jacob's sons did (Genesis 47:4). The family means to stay only until the famine ends.

decisions.choice: the fields of Moab: the open country of Moab
decisions.reason: The word for "field" here means the open land or territory of a people (Genesis 32:4; Numbers 21:20). Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, a few days' walk from Bethlehem.

decisions.choice: the judges judged (Literal, Balanced); judges led Israel (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in Judges, Readable says "led" so a new reader does not picture judges in a court; it adds "Israel", which the phrase means.

decisions.choice: live for a while as an outsider; the country of Moab
decisions.reason: Balanced follows the project's wording for a resident outsider; "country" says what "fields" means here. Literal keeps "sojourn" and "fields".

source.text: וְשֵׁ֣ם הָאִ֣ישׁ אֱֽלִימֶ֡לֶךְ וְשֵׁם֩ אִשְׁתּ֨וֹ נָעֳמִ֜י וְשֵׁ֥ם שְׁנֵֽי־בָנָ֣יו׀מַחְל֤וֹן וְכִלְיוֹן֙ אֶפְרָתִ֔ים מִבֵּ֥ית לֶ֖חֶם יְהוּדָ֑ה וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ שְׂדֵי־מוֹאָ֖ב וַיִּֽהְיוּ־שָֽׁם׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] name of the man [was] Elimelech, and [the] name of his wife Naomi, and [the] name of [the] two of his sons Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites from Bethlehem [of] Judah; and they came [to the] fields of Moab and were there.

en.L: And the name of the man was Elimelech, and the name of his wife was Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. And they came to the fields of Moab and remained there.
en.B: The man was called Elimelech, his wife was called Naomi, and his two sons were called Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They came into the country of Moab and settled there.
en.R: The man's name was Elimelech, and his wife's name was Naomi. Their two sons were named Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites, from Bethlehem in Judah. They arrived in Moab and stayed there.

decisions.choice: Ephrathites: people of Ephrath, the district of Bethlehem
decisions.reason: Ephrath is an old name for Bethlehem or the area around it (Genesis 35:19; 48:7; Micah 5:1). David's father Jesse is called "an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah" in the same words (1 Samuel 17:12), so the name already points toward the end of the book (4:11, 17).

decisions.choice: the names: Elimelech "my God is king", Naomi "pleasant"; Mahlon and Chilion perhaps "sickness" and "failing"
decisions.reason: Elimelech means "my God is king", a striking name in a time with no king (Judges 21:25). Naomi means "pleasant" or "my pleasantness", and she plays on it in verse 20. Mahlon and Chilion sound like words for being sick and for coming to an end, which fits their early deaths, but the meaning of these two names is not certain and the text does not comment on them.

decisions.choice: settled there; stayed there
decisions.reason: "Were there" means they lived there; Balanced and Readable say so. Literal has "remained there".

source.text: וַיָּ֥מָת אֱלִימֶ֖לֶךְ אִ֣ישׁ נָעֳמִ֑י וַתִּשָּׁאֵ֥ר הִ֖יא וּשְׁנֵ֥י בָנֶֽיהָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And died Elimelech, [the] husband of Naomi, and she was left, she and her two sons.

en.L: And Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left, she and her two sons.
en.B: Then Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, leaving her with her two sons.
en.R: Then Naomi's husband Elimelech died. Naomi was left with only her two sons.

decisions.choice: she was left: the first of Naomi's losses
decisions.reason: The same verb returns in verse 5, when she is left without her sons as well. The narrator tells the story from Naomi's side: each death is counted as a loss to her.

decisions.choice: left with only her two sons
decisions.reason: "Only" brings out that her husband was now gone and her sons were all the family she had; the Hebrew implies it by setting "she and her two sons" after the death.

source.text: וַיִּשְׂא֣וּ לָהֶ֗ם נָשִׁים֙ מֹֽאֲבִיּ֔וֹת שֵׁ֤ם הָֽאַחַת֙ עָרְפָּ֔ה וְשֵׁ֥ם הַשֵּׁנִ֖ית ר֑וּת וַיֵּ֥שְׁבוּ שָׁ֖ם כְּעֶ֥שֶׂר שָׁנִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And they took for themselves wives, Moabite [women]; [the] name of the one [was] Orpah, and [the] name of the second Ruth; and they lived there about ten years.

en.L: And they took for themselves Moabite wives; the name of the one was Orpah, and the name of the second was Ruth. And they lived there about ten years.
en.B: The sons married Moabite women, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. They lived there for about ten years.
en.R: Both sons married women from Moab. One was named Orpah, and the other was named Ruth. The family lived in Moab for about ten years.

decisions.choice: took wives: married
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to lift or carry; with "wives" it means to marry, a way of saying it found mostly in later books (Ezra 10:44; 2 Chronicles 11:21).

decisions.choice: Moabite women: wives from a people outside Israel
decisions.reason: Moab was a neighbor with a troubled history with Israel (Numbers 22-25), and the law kept Moabites out of the LORD's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:4). The narrator does not comment on the marriages; the question of a Moabite woman joining Israel is the heart of the story (1:16; 2:10-12; 4:10).

decisions.choice: about ten years: the length of the stay in Moab
decisions.reason: The ten years are counted after the marriages, but they may cover the family's whole time in Moab. Either way, the marriages had produced no children (4:13 is Ruth's first child).

decisions.choice: The sons (Balanced); Both sons (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "they"; Balanced and Readable name who married, so a reader does not think of Naomi.

source.text: וַיָּמ֥וּתוּ גַם־שְׁנֵיהֶ֖ם מַחְל֣וֹן וְכִלְי֑וֹן וַתִּשָּׁאֵר֙ הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה מִשְּׁנֵ֥י יְלָדֶ֖יהָ וּמֵאִישָֽׁהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And died also [the] two of them, Mahlon and Chilion, and was left the woman without her two children and without her husband.

en.L: And both of them also died, Mahlon and Chilion, and the woman was left without her two children and without her husband.
en.B: Then both Mahlon and Chilion died as well, and the woman was left alone, without her two sons and without her husband.
en.R: Then Mahlon and Chilion died too. Naomi had lost both her sons and her husband.

decisions.choice: her two children: her sons, seen as her children
decisions.reason: The word means a young child or boy, though the sons were grown and married. It looks at them as Naomi's children, the ones she bore. The same word is used for the child Naomi holds at the end of the book (4:16), when what she lost is restored.

decisions.choice: the woman was left: Naomi alone
decisions.reason: She is not named here but called "the woman", which makes her stand alone in the scene. The verb "was left" repeats verse 3: now no man of her family remains.

decisions.choice: sons
decisions.reason: "Children" in English would suggest small children; Balanced and Readable say "sons". Literal keeps "children".

decisions.choice: left alone (Balanced); Naomi (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "alone", which the two "without" phrases mean; Readable names "the woman" so a new reader knows who is meant.

source.text: וַתָּ֤קָם הִיא֙ וְכַלֹּתֶ֔יהָ וַתָּ֖שָׁב מִשְּׂדֵ֣י מוֹאָ֑ב כִּ֤י שָֽׁמְעָה֙ בִּשְׂדֵ֣ה מוֹאָ֔ב כִּֽי־פָקַ֤ד יְהוָה֙ אֶת־עַמּ֔וֹ לָתֵ֥ת לָהֶ֖ם לָֽחֶם׃

records.literal_gloss: And she arose, she and her daughters-in-law, and she returned from [the] fields of Moab, for she had heard in [the] field of Moab that YHWH had visited his people to give to them bread.

en.L: And she arose with her daughters-in-law and turned back from the fields of Moab, for she had heard in the field of Moab that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had visited {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people to give them bread.
en.B: Then she got ready with her daughters-in-law to go back from the country of Moab, because she had heard there that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had come to the help of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people and given them food.
en.R: While she was still in Moab, Naomi heard that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had cared for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people by giving them food again. So she and her daughters-in-law got ready to leave Moab and go back home.

decisions.choice: visited his people: came to care for them
decisions.reason: The verb means to give attention to someone, to look after them. When God "visits" his people he steps in to help them (Genesis 21:1; 50:24; Exodus 4:31). Here his help is the end of the famine.

decisions.choice: bread: food, the harvest
decisions.reason: The word means bread and so food in general. It answers the famine of verse 1 and echoes the name Bethlehem, "house of bread".

decisions.choice: returned: began the journey back
decisions.reason: The verb "return" (or "turn back") is the key word of the chapter and appears again and again (verses 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22). Here it names the start of the journey; verse 22 tells its end.

decisions.choice: food
decisions.reason: In English "bread" would sound like one food only; Balanced and Readable say "food". Literal keeps "bread".

decisions.choice: news first, then the journey; "again"
decisions.reason: Readable tells what Naomi heard before what she did, the order in which things happened. "Again" makes clear that the famine had ended.

source.text: וַתֵּצֵ֗א מִן־הַמָּקוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיְתָה־שָׁ֔מָּה וּשְׁתֵּ֥י כַלֹּתֶ֖יהָ עִמָּ֑הּ וַתֵּלַ֣כְנָה בַדֶּ֔רֶךְ לָשׁ֖וּב אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ יְהוּדָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And she went out from the place where she had been there, and [the] two of her daughters-in-law with her, and they went on the way to return to [the] land of Judah.

en.L: And she went out from the place where she had been, and her two daughters-in-law with her, and they went on the road to return to the land of Judah.
en.B: She set out from the place where she had been living, with her two daughters-in-law, and they took the road back to the land of Judah.
en.R: She left the place where she had been living, and her two daughters-in-law went with her. They started down the road that led back to Judah.

decisions.choice: to return to the land of Judah: Naomi's return, which the young women share for now
decisions.reason: The young widows are Moabites and have never lived in Judah, yet they are on the road "to return" with her. The word belongs to Naomi's journey; whether the two women will truly go with her is the question of the next verses.

decisions.choice: took the road back (Balanced); started down the road that led back (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Went on the way to return" means they had begun the journey; Balanced and Readable say so.

source.text: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר נָעֳמִי֙ לִשְׁתֵּ֣י כַלֹּתֶ֔יהָ לֵ֣כְנָה שֹּׁ֔בְנָה אִשָּׁ֖ה לְבֵ֣ית אִמָּ֑הּ יַ֣עַשׂ יְהוָ֤ה עִמָּכֶם֙ חֶ֔סֶד כַּאֲשֶׁ֧ר עֲשִׂיתֶ֛ם עִם־הַמֵּתִ֖ים וְעִמָּדִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Naomi to [the] two of her daughters-in-law, go, return, each woman to [the] house of her mother; may deal YHWH with you steadfast love as you have dealt with the dead and with me.

en.L: And Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, return, each of you to her mother's house. May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} deal with you in steadfast love, as you have dealt with the dead and with me.
en.B: But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go home, both of you, each to the house of your mother. May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} show you faithful love, just as you showed it to the men who died and to me.
en.R: Then Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "You should both go back home to your mothers. You have shown faithful love to your husbands who died and to me. May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} show the same faithful love to you.

decisions.choice: steadfast love: loyal goodness that keeps faith with others
decisions.reason: Chesed is goodness shown out of loyalty, more than duty requires, to someone to whom one is bound. It is used of the LORD's covenant love (Exodus 34:6) and of people keeping faith with each other (Joshua 2:12). The young women have kept faith with their husbands and with Naomi; Naomi asks the LORD to keep faith with them in the same way. The word comes back at key points of the book (2:20; 3:10), and the story shows it lived out.

decisions.choice: her mother's house: home, where a new marriage would be arranged
decisions.reason: A widow usually went back to her "father's house" (Genesis 38:11; Leviticus 22:13). "Mother's house" is rarer and is used where marriage is in view (Genesis 24:28; Song of Songs 3:4; 8:2). Naomi is sending them home to marry again, as verse 9 says.

decisions.choice: may he deal: the short form of the verb, marking a wish
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the text (ketiv) give the long form of the verb "he will do"; the reading the scribes marked (qere) is the short form used for a wish. Either way Naomi is praying for the women; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: you: the women addressed with masculine plural forms
decisions.reason: Several words addressed to the two women have masculine plural endings (here and in verses 9, 11 and 13). Hebrew sometimes uses these forms for a group of women, and the book does so more than once (4:11); it does not change who is meant.

decisions.choice: steadfast love (Literal); faithful love (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in Exodus 34:6, Deuteronomy and Joshua 2:12, so that the loyalty in the word is kept; "kindness" alone would leave it out. The same wording is kept at every occurrence in Ruth (2:20; 3:10).

decisions.choice: what they have done first, then the wish; "your husbands"
decisions.reason: Readable tells what the women have done before Naomi's prayer, so the "same faithful love" is clear. "The dead" are first of all the women's husbands (verse 5), so Readable names them.

source.text: יִתֵּ֤ן יְהוָה֙ לָכֶ֔ם וּמְצֶ֣אןָ מְנוּחָ֔ה אִשָּׁ֖ה בֵּ֣ית אִישָׁ֑הּ וַתִּשַּׁ֣ק לָהֶ֔ן וַתִּשֶּׂ֥אנָה קוֹלָ֖ן וַתִּבְכֶּֽינָה׃

records.literal_gloss: May give YHWH to you, and find rest, each woman [in the] house of her husband. And she kissed them, and they lifted their voice and wept.

en.L: May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} grant you that you find rest, each in the house of her husband." And she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept.
en.B: May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} grant that each of you finds rest in the home of a new husband." Then she kissed them, and they wept aloud.
en.R: May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} give each of you a husband and a safe, settled home." Then Naomi kissed them goodbye, and they all cried loudly.

decisions.choice: may the LORD grant you that you find rest: a wish in short form
alternatives: may the LORD give you husbands, and may you find rest
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "may the LORD give to you, and find rest": what the LORD is to give is the finding of rest itself. Some read an unspoken object ("give you husbands"), but the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: rest: a settled, secure home
decisions.reason: "Rest" here is the security of a home and a husband after the losses of widowhood. Naomi seeks the same "rest" for Ruth in Israel later (3:1).

decisions.choice: lifted their voice and wept: cried aloud
decisions.reason: Raising the voice and weeping is open, loud grief (Genesis 21:16; 29:11), here the grief of parting.

decisions.choice: a new husband (Balanced); a husband and a safe, settled home (Readable)
decisions.reason: Their first husbands are dead, so the "house of her husband" is a new marriage; Balanced says "new". Readable spells out what "rest" in a husband's house means.

decisions.choice: wept aloud; kissed them goodbye, cried loudly
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what lifting the voice means; Readable adds "goodbye", since this is a farewell kiss.

source.text: וַתֹּאמַ֖רְנָה־לָּ֑הּ כִּי־אִתָּ֥ךְ נָשׁ֖וּב לְעַמֵּֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And they said to her, no, with you we will return to your people.

en.L: And they said to her, "No, we will return with you to your people."
en.B: They said to her, "No! We will go back with you to your people."
en.R: But they told her, "No! We will go with you to your people."

decisions.choice: no: rather, a refusal
alternatives: surely we will return with you
decisions.reason: The small word that opens their answer here sets what follows against Naomi's command: not what she says, but this. It is a refusal, "No, we will return with you."

decisions.choice: we will return: going with Naomi as if going home
decisions.reason: The young women use Naomi's word "return" for a land they have never seen. They speak as if her people were already theirs.

decisions.choice: go with you
decisions.reason: "Go back" would puzzle a new reader, since they had never been in Judah; Readable says "go". Literal and Balanced keep the return.

source.text: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר נָעֳמִי֙ שֹׁ֣בְנָה בְנֹתַ֔י לָ֥מָּה תֵלַ֖כְנָה עִמִּ֑י הַֽעֽוֹד־לִ֤י בָנִים֙ בְּֽמֵעַ֔י וְהָי֥וּ לָכֶ֖ם לַאֲנָשִֽׁים׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Naomi, return, my daughters; why will you go with me? [Are there] still to me sons in my inward parts, and they will be for you for husbands?

en.L: And Naomi said, "Return, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Are there still sons in my womb, that they might become husbands for you?
en.B: But Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters. Why go with me? Do I still have sons inside my womb who could become your husbands?
en.R: Naomi answered, "Go back home, my daughters. Why should you come with me? I cannot give birth to more sons who could become your husbands.

decisions.choice: sons to become your husbands: the custom of a brother marrying his dead brother's widow
decisions.reason: Naomi's question assumes the custom that when a man died without a son, his brother married the widow to give the dead man a son and an heir (Genesis 38:8; Deuteronomy 25:5-10). Naomi has no more sons to give, so the young women have nothing to hope for in her family. The custom matters again in chapter 4 (4:5, 10).

decisions.choice: my daughters: a word of affection for her daughters-in-law
decisions.reason: Naomi calls her sons' wives "my daughters" (also verses 12-13), and Boaz calls Ruth "my daughter" (2:8). It shows the family bond between them.

decisions.choice: in my inward parts: in my womb
decisions.reason: The word means the inner parts of the body, here the womb (Genesis 25:23).

decisions.choice: a statement in place of the question
decisions.reason: Naomi's question expects the answer no; Readable says it as a plain statement so a young reader does not miss the point.

source.text: שֹׁ֤בְנָה בְנֹתַי֙ לֵ֔כְןָ כִּ֥י זָקַ֖נְתִּי מִהְי֣וֹת לְאִ֑ישׁ כִּ֤י אָמַ֨רְתִּי֙ יֶשׁ־לִ֣י תִקְוָ֔ה גַּ֣ם הָיִ֤יתִי הַלַּ֨יְלָה֙ לְאִ֔ישׁ וְגַ֖ם יָלַ֥דְתִּי בָנִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Return, my daughters, go, for I am [too] old to be to a husband. If I said, there is to me hope, even [if] I were this night to a husband, and also bore sons,

en.L: Return, my daughters, go, for I am too old to have a husband. If I said, 'I have hope,' even if I had a husband tonight and also bore sons,
en.B: Go back, my daughters, go on your way, for I am too old to marry again. Even if I thought there was still hope for me, even if I had a husband tonight and then gave birth to sons,
en.R: Go back, my daughters. Go! I am too old to marry again. Suppose I told myself there was still hope for me. Suppose I married tonight and later had sons.

decisions.choice: if I said ... even if ...: a run of conditions that verse 13 answers
decisions.reason: Naomi piles up impossible conditions ("if I said I had hope, even if I had a husband tonight, and even if I bore sons") and only gives her answer in verse 13: they could not wait that long. The sentence runs into the next verse.

decisions.choice: to be to a husband: to marry, to be a man's wife
decisions.reason: "To be to a man" means to become a man's wife (Leviticus 21:3; Deuteronomy 24:2). In the second use, "this night", it means to be with a husband at once.

decisions.choice: this night: tonight, at once
decisions.reason: Naomi imagines the quickest case possible: marrying this very night. Even then sons would come far too late.

decisions.choice: Suppose ... Suppose ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns the long chain of conditions into short sentences beginning "Suppose"; verse 13 gives the answer.

source.text: הֲלָהֵ֣ן׀תְּשַׂבֵּ֗רְנָה עַ֚ד אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִגְדָּ֔לוּ הֲלָהֵן֙ תֵּֽעָגֵ֔נָה לְבִלְתִּ֖י הֱי֣וֹת לְאִ֑ישׁ אַ֣ל בְּנֹתַ֗י כִּֽי־מַר־לִ֤י מְאֹד֙ מִכֶּ֔ם כִּֽי־יָצְאָ֥ה בִ֖י יַד־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: therefore would you wait until that they grew up? therefore would you shut yourselves off so as not to be to a husband? No, my daughters, for [it is] bitter to me very [much] more than you, for has gone out against me [the] hand of YHWH.

en.L: would you therefore wait until they grew up? Would you therefore shut yourselves away so as not to have a husband? No, my daughters, for it is far more bitter for me than for you, for the hand of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has gone out against me."
en.B: would you then wait until they had grown up? Would you then keep yourselves from marrying? No, my daughters! My lot is far more bitter than yours, for the hand of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has turned against me."
en.R: Would you wait for them to grow up? Would you stay unmarried all that time? No, my daughters. My life is much more bitter than yours, because {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has turned {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand against me."

decisions.choice: therefore: then, in that case
decisions.reason: The short word that opens both questions is best read as "therefore" or "then", as in Aramaic. Others read it as "for them" ("would you wait for them?"); the question is the same either way.

decisions.choice: shut yourselves off: hold back from marriage
decisions.reason: The verb is found only here in the Bible. From related words it means to be kept back or shut in, here kept from marrying, living as a widow with no husband.

decisions.choice: it is far more bitter for me than for you
alternatives: it is very bitter for me because of you
decisions.reason: The words can be read as a comparison ("more bitter for me than for you": the young women can still marry, Naomi cannot) or as "it is very bitter for me because of you" (she grieves over what has happened to them). The comparison fits what follows, that the LORD's hand is against her.

decisions.choice: the hand of the LORD has gone out against me
decisions.reason: The LORD's hand is his power at work, here in judgment or hardship (Exodus 9:3; Deuteronomy 2:15; Judges 2:15). Naomi sees her losses as coming from the LORD himself. She says it more strongly in verses 20-21; the story does not take back her complaint, but it goes on to show the LORD's care.

decisions.choice: My lot (Balanced); My life (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "it is bitter for me"; Balanced and Readable name what is bitter.

source.text: וַתִּשֶּׂ֣נָה קוֹלָ֔ן וַתִּבְכֶּ֖ינָה ע֑וֹד וַתִּשַּׁ֤ק עָרְפָּה֙ לַחֲמוֹתָ֔הּ וְר֖וּת דָּ֥בְקָה בָּֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And they lifted their voice and wept again; and kissed Orpah her mother-in-law, and Ruth clung to her.

en.L: And they lifted up their voices and wept again. And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her.
en.B: Again they wept aloud. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth held on to her.
en.R: The women cried loudly again. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye and left. But Ruth held on tight to Naomi.

decisions.choice: Orpah kissed her mother-in-law: a farewell
decisions.reason: A kiss on parting was a goodbye (Genesis 31:28; 1 Kings 19:20). Orpah does as Naomi asks and goes home; the text does not blame her (Naomi wished her well in verses 8-9).

decisions.choice: clung: held fast, a word for lasting loyalty
decisions.reason: The verb means to stick to or hold fast. It is used of a man holding to his wife (Genesis 2:24) and of Israel holding to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20). Ruth's act says what her words in verses 16-17 then put into an oath.

decisions.choice: but Ruth: the two women set side by side
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts Ruth's name before the verb, setting her against Orpah: one kissed and left, the other held on.

decisions.choice: goodbye (Balanced, Readable); and left (Readable)
decisions.reason: The kiss is a farewell, and verse 15 says Orpah has gone back; Readable says so here.

source.text: וַתֹּ֗אמֶר הִנֵּה֙ שָׁ֣בָה יְבִמְתֵּ֔ךְ אֶל־עַמָּ֖הּ וְאֶל־אֱלֹהֶ֑יהָ שׁ֖וּבִי אַחֲרֵ֥י יְבִמְתֵּֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And she said, look, has returned your sister-in-law to her people and to her gods; return after your sister-in-law.

en.L: And she said, "Look, your sister-in-law has returned to her people and to her gods. Return after your sister-in-law."
en.B: Naomi said, "See, your sister-in-law has turned back, home to her people and her gods. Follow your sister-in-law back."
en.R: Naomi said, "Look! Your sister-in-law has gone back to her own people and her own gods. You should go back with her."

decisions.choice: her gods: the gods of Moab
decisions.reason: The plural word can mean "gods" or, of Israel's God, "God". Here it is the god or gods of Moab, chiefly Chemosh (Numbers 21:29; 1 Kings 11:33). Going home meant going back to Moab's worship as well; Ruth's answer in verse 16 turns on this.

decisions.choice: sister-in-law: the widow of her husband's brother
decisions.reason: The word is used for the wife of one's husband's brother, the same family word found in the law of a brother's widow (Deuteronomy 25:7, 9).

decisions.choice: Naomi said
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "she said"; Balanced and Readable name Naomi so the speaker is clear.

source.text: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר רוּת֙ אַל־תִּפְגְּעִי־בִ֔י לְעָזְבֵ֖ךְ לָשׁ֣וּב מֵאַחֲרָ֑יִךְ כִּ֠י אֶל־אֲשֶׁ֨ר תֵּלְכִ֜י אֵלֵ֗ךְ וּבַאֲשֶׁ֤ר תָּלִ֨ינִי֙ אָלִ֔ין עַמֵּ֣ךְ עַמִּ֔י וֵאלֹהַ֖יִךְ אֱלֹהָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Ruth, do not urge me to leave you, to turn back from after you; for to where you go I will go, and in where you lodge I will lodge; your people my people, and your God my God.

en.L: And Ruth said, "Do not press me to abandon you, to turn back from following you. For to the place you go, I will go, and in the place you lodge, I will lodge. Your people [are] my people, and your God [is] my God.
en.B: But Ruth said, "Stop pressing me to leave you and turn away from following you. Wherever you travel, I will travel with you; wherever you stop for the night, I will stop as well. Your people are now my people, and your God is now my God.
en.R: But Ruth answered, "Do not ask me to leave you or to turn back and stop following you. I am going with you, wherever that takes me. Wherever you sleep, I will sleep too. From now on your people are my people, and your God is my God.

decisions.choice: urge me: press me with requests
decisions.reason: The verb means to meet someone, and so to press them with a request (Genesis 23:8). Naomi has urged her three times (verses 8, 11-13, 15); Ruth asks her to stop.

decisions.choice: lodge: spend the night
decisions.reason: The verb means to stay for the night. On the road it is each night's stop; beyond the road it is wherever Naomi will live.

decisions.choice: your people my people, and your God my God: a declaration with no verb
alternatives: your people will be my people, and your God will be my God
decisions.reason: Hebrew can join two nouns with no verb between them. Ruth's words state what is true from this moment and for the future: she belongs to Naomi's people and takes Naomi's God as her own. The pledge is built from short balanced pairs, ending in the oath of verse 17.

decisions.choice: your God my God: Ruth takes the God of Israel as her own
decisions.reason: Orpah has gone back "to her gods" (verse 15); Ruth chooses the God of Naomi, the LORD, by whose name she swears in verse 17. Boaz later speaks of her as one who has come to take refuge under the LORD's wings (2:12).

decisions.choice: are now (Balanced); From now on (Readable)
decisions.reason: With no verb in the Hebrew, Balanced and Readable say "now" to show the declaration takes effect from this moment; Literal brackets the supplied verb.

source.text: בַּאֲשֶׁ֤ר תָּמ֨וּתִי֙ אָמ֔וּת וְשָׁ֖ם אֶקָּבֵ֑ר כֹּה֩ יַעֲשֶׂ֨ה יְהוָ֥ה לִי֙ וְכֹ֣ה יֹסִ֔יף כִּ֣י הַמָּ֔וֶת יַפְרִ֖יד בֵּינִ֥י וּבֵינֵֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: In where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. Thus may do YHWH to me, and thus may he add, if death will separate between me and between you.

en.L: In the place you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. Thus may {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} do to me, and more also, if [anything but] death separates me from you."
en.B: The place where you die is where I will die and be buried. May {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} deal with me ever so severely if anything except death comes between us."
en.R: I will die where you die, and be buried in the same place. I make this solemn promise before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: only death will separate us. If I break it, may {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} punish me severely."

decisions.choice: there I will be buried: belonging for life and death
decisions.reason: To be buried in a land and with a family was to belong to it for good (Genesis 47:29-30; 50:25). Ruth will not even go back to Moab to be buried.

decisions.choice: thus may the LORD do to me and thus may he add: an oath that calls down a curse on oneself
decisions.reason: This is a set form of oath (1 Samuel 3:17; 2 Samuel 3:9; 1 Kings 19:2). The speaker asks God to punish them, and more besides, if they break their word; the punishment is left unspoken. Ruth swears by the LORD, the God of Israel.

decisions.choice: if anything but death separates me from you
alternatives: if even death separates me from you
decisions.reason: After this oath the small word that follows gives what is sworn. It can be read "if anything but death separates us" (only death will part them) or "if even death separates us" (not even death will, since she will be buried beside Naomi). Both make the pledge as strong as possible; the first fits the plain sense of the words best.

decisions.choice: [anything but] (Literal); anything except (Balanced); only death (Readable)
decisions.reason: The words supplied give the reading chosen in m3; Literal brackets them.

decisions.choice: the promise first, then the curse
decisions.reason: Readable says what Ruth promises before the self-curse, and explains the oath form in plain words.

source.text: וַתֵּ֕רֶא כִּֽי־מִתְאַמֶּ֥צֶת הִ֖יא לָלֶ֣כֶת אִתָּ֑הּ וַתֶּחְדַּ֖ל לְדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלֶֽיהָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And she saw that determined [was] she to go with her, and she ceased to speak to her.

en.L: And she saw that she was determined to go with her, and she stopped speaking to her.
en.B: When Naomi saw that Ruth was set on going with her, she said no more to her.
en.R: Naomi saw that Ruth had made up her mind to go with her. So Naomi stopped arguing with her.

decisions.choice: determined: had made herself firm
decisions.reason: The verb means to make oneself strong or firm; here Ruth's mind is set and cannot be moved (compare 2 Chronicles 13:7).

decisions.choice: she stopped speaking to her: Naomi ended her pleading
decisions.reason: Naomi stops urging Ruth to go back. Nothing is said of her answer; she says no word to Ruth until they reach Bethlehem, and there she speaks as if she had come home "empty" (verse 21).

decisions.choice: Naomi ... Ruth
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "she" and "her"; Balanced and Readable name the two women.

decisions.choice: stopped arguing with her
decisions.reason: Readable says what Naomi's speaking had been: trying to persuade Ruth to go back.

source.text: וַתֵּלַ֣כְנָה שְׁתֵּיהֶ֔ם עַד־בֹּאָ֖נָה בֵּ֣ית לָ֑חֶם וַיְהִ֗י כְּבֹאָ֨נָה֙ בֵּ֣ית לֶ֔חֶם וַתֵּהֹ֤ם כָּל־הָעִיר֙ עֲלֵיהֶ֔ן וַתֹּאמַ֖רְנָה הֲזֹ֥את נָעֳמִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And they went, [the] two of them, until they came [to] Bethlehem. And it was, as they came [to] Bethlehem, and was stirred all the town over them, and they said, [is] this Naomi?

en.L: And the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. And it happened, as they came to Bethlehem, that the whole town was stirred over them, and they said, "Is this Naomi?"
en.B: So the two of them traveled on until they reached Bethlehem. When they arrived, the whole town was in an uproar over them, and the women said, "Can this be Naomi?"
en.R: The two women walked on until they reached Bethlehem. When they arrived, the whole town was excited about them. The women there asked, "Is this really Naomi?"

decisions.choice: was stirred: was in an uproar
decisions.reason: The verb is used of a crowd or a town in commotion (1 Samuel 4:5; 1 Kings 1:45). Their arrival is the talk of the town; the word does not say whether the stir was joy or shock.

decisions.choice: they said: the women of the town
decisions.reason: The verb is feminine plural: the women of Bethlehem speak. They speak again at the end of the book, when they bless Naomi over her grandson (4:14-17).

decisions.choice: Is this Naomi? astonishment at how she has changed
decisions.reason: The question is surprise rather than a request for her name: after some ten years and her losses, she is hardly the woman they knew. Naomi's answer in verses 20-21 takes it that way.

decisions.choice: the women
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say who spoke, as the feminine verb does; Literal keeps "they".

source.text: וַתֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֔ן אַל־תִּקְרֶ֥אנָה לִ֖י נָעֳמִ֑י קְרֶ֤אןָ לִי֙ מָרָ֔א כִּי־הֵמַ֥ר שַׁדַּ֛י לִ֖י מְאֹֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And she said to them, do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for has made bitter [the] Almighty to me very [much].

en.L: And she said to them, "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.
en.B: She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi. Call me Mara, for the Almighty has made my life very bitter.
en.R: Naomi told them, "Do not call me Naomi, which means 'pleasant.' Call me Mara, which means 'bitter.' God All-Powerful has made my life very bitter.

decisions.choice: Naomi "pleasant", Mara "bitter": a new name for a changed life
decisions.reason: Naomi means "pleasant" or "my pleasantness"; Mara means "bitter", from the same root as "has made bitter" in this verse and "bitter" in verse 13. She asks to be named for what has happened to her. No one in the story calls her Mara; she is Naomi to the end (4:17).

decisions.choice: the Almighty: Shaddai, an ancient name of God
decisions.reason: Shaddai is a very old name for God, used with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3). Its first meaning is not certain; "the Almighty" is the long-standing sense. In Job it is the name of the God who sends both good and suffering, and Job uses almost Naomi's words: "the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter" (Job 27:2).

decisions.choice: the Almighty has dealt bitterly with me: Naomi lays her loss at God's door
decisions.reason: Naomi does not deny God's rule; she holds to it and complains of it, as Job and many psalms do. The story does not rebuke her; it goes on to show the same God bringing her blessing (4:14-15).

decisions.choice: the Almighty (Literal, Balanced); God All-Powerful (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in Numbers, Readable puts the name in plain words.

decisions.choice: which means 'pleasant'; which means 'bitter'
decisions.reason: The point of Naomi's words lies in the meaning of the names; Readable gives it in the text so a reader without a footnote can follow.

source.text: אֲנִי֙ מְלֵאָ֣ה הָלַ֔כְתִּי וְרֵיקָ֖ם הֱשִׁיבַ֣נִי יְהוָ֑ה לָ֣מָּה תִקְרֶ֤אנָה לִי֙ נָעֳמִ֔י וַֽיהוָה֙ עָ֣נָה בִ֔י וְשַׁדַּ֖י הֵ֥רַֽעלִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: I full went, and empty has brought me back YHWH; why do you call me Naomi, and YHWH has testified against me, and [the] Almighty has done harm to me?

en.L: I went away full, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has brought me back empty. Why do you call me Naomi, when {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has testified against me and the Almighty has done me harm?"
en.B: I went away full, but {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has brought me home empty. Why call me Naomi? {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has testified against me, and the Almighty has brought disaster on me."
en.R: When I left here, my life was full. Now {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has brought me back with nothing. So why call me Naomi? {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has spoken against me. God All-Powerful has brought trouble on me."

decisions.choice: full ... empty: with a family, and without one
decisions.reason: Naomi left in a famine, so "full" is not wealth but her husband and two sons; "empty" is their loss. The Hebrew puts both words first for weight. Yet Ruth stands beside her as she speaks, and later Boaz will not send Ruth back to Naomi "empty" (3:17).

decisions.choice: has testified against me: has spoken as a witness against me
decisions.reason: With these vowels the verb means to answer or testify, and "against me" makes it a witness's word in a lawsuit (Exodus 20:16; Numbers 35:30). Naomi feels the LORD has spoken against her. The same letters can be read as "has afflicted me", as the ancient Greek translation does; the sense of hardship from God is the same.

decisions.choice: the Almighty has done harm to me
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring harm or trouble on someone. Naomi uses the two names of God side by side, the LORD and the Almighty (see verse 20), and holds him to account for her losses.

decisions.choice: has spoken against me
decisions.reason: Readable says in plain words what testifying against someone is.

decisions.choice: brought disaster (Balanced); brought trouble (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "done me harm"; Balanced and Readable use words for misfortune, since the verb here speaks of what happened to her, not of wrongdoing.

decisions.choice: the Almighty (Literal, Balanced); God All-Powerful (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 20.

source.text: וַתָּ֣שָׁב נָעֳמִ֗י וְר֨וּת הַמּוֹאֲבִיָּ֤ה כַלָּתָהּ֙ עִמָּ֔הּ הַשָּׁ֖בָה מִשְּׂדֵ֣י מוֹאָ֑ב וְהֵ֗מָּה בָּ֚אוּ בֵּ֣ית לֶ֔חֶם בִּתְחִלַּ֖ת קְצִ֥יר שְׂעֹרִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And returned Naomi, and Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, with her, who returned from [the] fields of Moab; and they came [to] Bethlehem at [the] beginning of [the] harvest of barley.

en.L: So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, with her, who returned from the fields of Moab. And they came to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
en.B: So Naomi came back, and with her came her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabite, who had come back from the country of Moab. They arrived in Bethlehem as the barley harvest was beginning.
en.R: That is how Naomi came back from Moab, with Ruth, her Moabite daughter-in-law, who came back with her. They reached Bethlehem just when people were starting to harvest the barley.

decisions.choice: who returned: said of Ruth
decisions.reason: The words most likely describe Ruth, the Moabite who "returned" from Moab though she had never lived in Judah, as she is described again in 2:6. The chapter's key word now includes her: Naomi's return is hers too.

decisions.choice: the beginning of the barley harvest: spring, the first grain harvest
decisions.reason: Barley ripened first, in spring about the time of Passover (Leviticus 23:10-11), before the wheat. The famine is over, the fields of Bethlehem are full, and the scene is set for chapter 2, where Ruth gleans in the harvest.

decisions.choice: returned ... at the beginning of harvest: the empty return meets a full land
decisions.reason: Naomi says she has come back empty (verse 21), but the chapter ends with Ruth at her side and the harvest beginning, the LORD's gift of food (verse 6). The story will move from emptiness to fullness.

decisions.choice: came back
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "came back" for both uses of "return", keeping the repeated word; Literal keeps "returned".
